After switch S is closed and the circuit becomes stable, both bulbs emit light normally. It is known that the self-inductance coefficient of the self-inductance coil is very large. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, two identical bulbs L1 and L2 are respectively connected in series with resistor R and self-inductance coil L, and connected to the two ends of a power supply. It is known that the self-inductance coefficient of the self-inductance coil is very large. After switch S is closed and before the circuit becomes stable, how does the brightness of bulb L1 change?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the left and right ends are respectively marked A and B, and there are parallel branches between A and B. In the upper branch, the self-inductance coil is marked L, with bulb L1 connected in series after it; in the middle branch, bulb L2 is connected in series after resistor R; below there is a power supply and switch S. Then reason: At the instant switch S is closed, because the self-inductance coefficient of self-inductance coil L is very large, it will strongly hinder the sudden increase of current in the upper branch, so the initial current through L1 is very small, and L1 is almost not bright. Afterwards the self-induction hindering effect gradually weakens, the current in the upper branch gradually increases, and the brightness of L1 also increases along with it, until after the circuit becomes stable it emits light normally. Therefore L1 gradually becomes brighter before stability.
